name: Motion Capture and Retargeting
title: Motion Capture and Retargeting
answer: Motion capture and retargeting covers recording human movement from sensors or video and mapping that movement onto a different body or character. In choreography and motion mapping, it lets a dancer's performance drive an avatar, a digital double, or an animated figure with different proportions. The scope includes capture hardware, skeletal solving, motion cleaning, and the transfer of joint rotations while preserving intent and timing. It sits between performance, animation, and machine learning, where the source motion is treated as data rather than a fixed recording.

sections.body: Motion capture and retargeting covers recording human movement from sensors or video and mapping that movement onto a different body or character. In choreography and motion mapping, it lets a dancer's performance drive an avatar, a digital double, or an animated figure with different proportions. The scope includes capture hardware, skeletal solving, motion cleaning, and the transfer of joint rotations while preserving intent and timing. It sits between performance, animation, and machine learning, where the source motion is treated as data rather than a fixed recording.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of optical marker systems, inertial suits, depth cameras, and plain video, depending on budget and capture volume. Processing typically happens on a workstation with a GPU for real-time preview or batch retargeting, and pipelines often use game engines or animation software to host the character rig. Cloud services are used for heavy training or batch processing, but live performance usually keeps capture and retargeting local to reduce latency.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical workflow captures joint positions or rotations, solves a skeleton, and then retargets that skeleton to a target rig by matching bone chains and adjusting for limb length and joint limits. Machine learning is increasingly used for markerless capture from video and for learning motion priors that make retargeting look natural on non-human bodies. The core craft is still in defining the mapping, cleaning foot slides and jitter, and preserving weight, phrasing, and contact with the floor.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on the performer whose motion is captured, the choreography being recorded, and the character or dataset that receives the motion. Consent to capture is not the same as consent to reuse, and a dancer's movement data can be personal data in some jurisdictions. Clear agreements should cover whether captured motion can be used to train models, stored in a library, or retargeted onto characters the performer has not approved. Provenance matters because retargeted motion can be copied and recombined in ways that make the original choreographer hard to trace.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward markerless capture from ordinary cameras and toward retargeting that works across very different body plans, such as human to quadruped or to abstract rigs. Real-time retargeting for live performance and virtual production is becoming more common, and generative models are starting to produce motion from text or music that can then be retargeted. The likely direction is a tighter loop between capture, editing, and performance, with less manual cleanup and more control over style and physical plausibility.
